name: Ife
info: Ifẹ̀, also called Ilé-Ifẹ̀, is an ancient Yoruba city in Osun State in south-western Nigeria, founded between 1000 and 500 BCE, a centre of sculpture and glass-making and the city Yoruba tradition holds to be the first.

facts.founded: Between 1000 BCE and 500 BCE. In Yoruba tradition the city was founded by order of the Supreme Deity Olódùmarè, and the earth on which it stands was made by Oduduwa.
facts.where: In Osun State in south-western Nigeria, about 218 kilometres north-east of Lagos, in a tropical savanna zone of undulating land, about 40 km from Osogbo.
facts.known: The Yoruba account of the creation of the world; the dynasty of Oduduwa and the Ọọ̀ni; the city of 401 deities and its festivals; naturalistic bronze, stone and terracotta sculpture; glass beads from Igbo Olokun; iron smelting
facts.today: Ife is a city in Osun State, Nigeria, the seat of the Ọọ̀ni of Ifẹ̀ and the site of Obafemi Awolowo University.

t: According to the traditions of the Yoruba religion, Ife was the first city, built on the earth that Oduduwa cast on the primordial ocean, and the kingdoms of Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Egba, Ijesha, Oyo and others were founded by his descendants.

The city was founded between 1000 and 500 BCE, was an important West African emporium by 900 CE, and reached a classical period in the 1100s in which its artists made naturalistic sculpture in terracotta, stone and copper alloy.
Production of that art declined after about 1400 as political and economic power shifted to Benin, but Ife remained the seat of the Ọọ̀ni and, in tradition, the city of 401 deities.
dyk: Ife glass beads have been found at sites as far away as Mali, Mauritania and Ghana, and Igbo Olokun may be one of the earliest glass-making workshops in West Africa.
ev: Ife is an important West African emporium producing sophisticated art forms

sections.origins:
Ifẹ̀ was founded sometime between 1000 BCE and 500 BCE. The city lies in what is now Osun State, in south-western Nigeria, on undulating land with deep clay soils on the upper slopes and sandy soils on the lower ones. Among the Yoruba the name is explained from the word ifẹ̀, which means expansion, so that Ilé-Ifẹ̀ is read as the land of expansion or, with ilé as house or home, the home of expansion.

The Yoruba religion gives the city a place in the making of the world. In the traditions of that religion Ilé-Ifẹ̀ was founded by the order of the Supreme Deity Olódùmarè, through Ọbatala. In the account told of the creation, Olódùmarè ordered Obatala to create the earth, but on the way he drank too much palm wine and became drunk. Oduduwa took the items of creation from him, descended from the abode of the Orisha on a chain and cast a handful of earth on the primordial ocean. The earth rose as a mound called Oke Ora, and a five-toed cockerel set on it scattered the earth around, making the land on which the first city would be built. Oduduwa planted a palm nut, from which sprang a tree with sixteen branches, a symbol of the 16 clans of the early Ife confederation.
sections.growth:
By 900 CE Ife had become an important West African emporium that produced sophisticated art forms, and by the 1100s it had entered a classical period and become the capital of a significant regional empire. It was a settlement of substantial size between the 12th and 14th centuries, with houses that had pavements of potsherds.

Its sculpture in bronze, stone and terracotta reached a peak between 1200 and 1400. Around 1300 the artists of Ife developed a refined and naturalistic tradition in terracotta, stone and copper alloy, many of the works apparently made under the patronage of King Obalufon II, who is identified today as the Yoruba patron deity of brass casting, weaving and regalia. Ife was also famous for its glass beads, found at sites as far away as Mali, Mauritania and Ghana, and glass bead making at Igbo Olokun was at its height between the 11th and 15th centuries. After the great period of its art, production declined as political and economic power shifted to the nearby kingdom of Benin, which, like the Yoruba kingdom of Oyo, grew into a major empire.
sections.rulers:
Yoruba tradition holds that Ilé-Ifẹ̀ fell into the hands of Oduduwa, the brother of Ọbatala, and that this created enmity between the two. Oduduwa created a dynasty there. The first Ọọ̀ni of Ifẹ̀ was a descendant of Oduduwa, who is counted as the 401st Orisha, and the sons and daughters of the dynasty became rulers of many other kingdoms in Yorubaland.

The same tradition names the kingdoms that Oduduwa's sons, daughters and grandchildren founded: Ila Orangun, Owu, Ketu, Sabe, Egba, Popo, Ijesha and Oyo, among others. Oranmiyan, Oduduwa's last born or, in another telling, his grandson, served as a minister and overseer of the nascent Edo kingdom. When he returned to Ile Ife he left behind a son, Eweka, born to an indigenous princess of Benin, and Eweka became the first widely accepted Oba of the second Edo dynasty. Oranmiyan later migrated north-westwards to found Oyo, which grew into an empire that at its height stretched from the western banks of the Niger to the eastern banks of the Volta, until its collapse in the mid 19th century.

The title of Ọọ̀ni is held to have passed to every king of Ife after Oduduwa. The 49th Ọọ̀ni was Adesoji Aderemi and the 50th Okunade Sijuwade, who died in 2015.
sections.life:
Ife is called the city of 401 deities, the irumole or orishas. Traditional worshippers are said to celebrate a festival of one of them on every day of the year. The festivals often last more than a day and combine the activities of priests in the palace with dramatic performances elsewhere in the kingdom. Historically the king appeared in public only at the annual Olojo festival, which celebrates the new dawn. Other major festivals are the Itapa festival for Obatala, the Edi festival for Moremi Ajasoro and the Ugbo festival with its Igare masqueraders. The rivalry of Oduduwa and Obatala is re-enacted by the followers of the two deities at the Itapa festival, which marks the new year.

The city had shrines and groves. Igbo Olokun, a forested sacred grove, housed shrines of the goddess Olokun and had glass makers who worked there. The Oduduwa shrine and grove is that of the progenitor of the Yoruba, and the Agbonniregun temple is the grove of Ọrunmila, the Orisha of wisdom, knowledge and divination. Artists often drew kings and gods with large heads, because they believed that ase, the inner power of a person, was held in the head. Excavations at Iyekere found stone tools, pottery and the remains of iron smelting, which was carried out in the Ife region.
sections.crises:
The Yoruba tradition records the conflict that followed the making of the world. When Oduduwa took the work of creation from Obatala, the usurpation gave rise to a lasting rivalry between the two Orisha, which their followers still re-enact.

The decline of Ife's sculpture is the one change in the city's fortunes that is dated, though only loosely. After the period between 1200 and 1400, the production of that art declined as political and economic power shifted to Benin, which grew into a major empire.

The glass-making of the Yoruba is said to have persisted into the seventeenth century in Osun Grove, and iron smelting in the Ife region has been placed, with caution, in the Late Iron Age before colonial rule. Colonisation by the British also affected the Ọọ̀ni: after it, no holder of the title had the international standing that the Ọọ̀ni acquired following the formation of the Yoruba Orisha Congress in 1986.
sections.legacy:
Ife is known worldwide for its ancient and naturalistic sculptures in bronze, stone and terracotta, which date to between 1200 and 1400 CE and are significant examples of naturalism in pre-colonial African art. They are distinguished by their variations in regalia, facial marking patterns and body proportions, and they include the life-size copper mask honouring Obalufon II, who is said to have invented bronze casting. The glass beads of Igbo Olokun are evidence of a glass industry that, by composition, was largely independent of glass-making traditions documented farther afield and took part in regional trade networks.

The city remains the holy city of the Yoruba, and the Ọọ̀ni is regarded as the chief priest and custodian of that city. The old palace was built of enamelled bricks and decorated with porcelain tiles and ornaments. Ife is today a city in Osun State, in Nigeria, about 218 kilometres north-east of Lagos, with two local government areas. It has a regional agricultural centre and is the home of Obafemi Awolowo University, formerly the University of Ife.

summary: Ifẹ̀ is an ancient Yoruba city in south-western Nigeria, founded between 1000 and 500 BCE and held by Yoruba tradition to be the first city. It was a regional capital and a centre of naturalistic sculpture and glass-making, and its Ọọ̀ni remains the chief priest of the Yoruba.
notes: START: the article says founded 'sometime between the years 1000 BC and 500 BC'. I used -1000 with circa true. Not a point date; editor may prefer -750.

TWO ACCOUNTS: the lead says Ile-Ife was founded by order of Olodumare by Obatala and then fell into the hands of Oduduwa; the History section says Oduduwa took the items of creation from the drunk Obatala. I gave both as tradition, side by side, without reconciling them.
Population: the lead says over 500,000 (2006 census), the Government section says an estimated 355,813. They disagree, so I left out all figures.
Oranmiyan: the article calls him Oduduwa's last born 'or grandson'; I kept the hedge.

The Ooni's lineage: the Traditional setting section says the dynasty traces to the city's founding 'more than ten thousand years before the birth of Jesus Christ'. That clashes with the 1000 to 500 BCE founding and was left out.

The Ooni 'the only one that speaks' and the 'igbakeji orisha' (second in command) claims were left out; the Ooni is described as the 401st Orisha only in the tradition's words about Oduduwa's descendant (the article is garbled on whether Oduduwa or the Ooni is the 401st).

Crises: the article gives no siege, sack, fire or plague. The crises section therefore rests on the Obatala rivalry, the decline of art, and glass and iron notes; the sentence 'The same article gives no siege, sack, fire or plague' speaks of the source and the editor should cut or reword it. Likewise the colonisation sentence is the article's only mention of British colonisation, undated.
Iyekere iron smelting is described as 'likely precolonial, during the Late Iron Age', with more excavation needed; hedged accordingly. Iyekere is not otherwise placed.

Glass: 'Glass production may have begun during, if not before, the 11th century' and peaked 11th to 15th; the Igbo Olokun section says 'between the 11th and 15th centuries AD'. Consistent. The article also says Osun Grove glass-making persisted into the seventeenth century.

Left out: climate, geography detail beyond the basics, notable people who are living or modern politicians and journalists, the Natural History Museum, schools, markets, the present Ooni's name and profession, the Olojo-era palace today, and the Orunmila healing claim.
Ife East and Ife Central: the article says two local government areas with 21 wards; I wrote only 'two local government areas'.

The article uses BC and AD; I wrote BCE and CE. The 'Ọọ̀ni acquired an international status' passage dates only to 1986; the article says he 'hadn't had' such standing 'since the city's colonisation by the British'. I kept that, undated.
